NEGRO SHOT BY DEPUTY RICHARDSON.
Ben Douglass Shot Through Shoulder By Officer Richardson When Resisting Arrest—Two Stories of the Shooting.
About 11 o'clock Tuesday night Officer H. C. Huffman and Deputy V. G. Richardson were called to the negro quarters on Upper Front street by a disturbance, which Ben Douglass, a negro who runs the pool room adjoining the O'Neal saloon, says was caused by some one breaking out the glass in his front door.

Douglass had fired a boy who worked for him, thinking the latter responsible for the broken glass, and was doing some loud talking when the officers came up and started to place him under arrest. Nothing was done at this time, however, and the officers returned about twelve.

Huffman states that Louis Skates made a move to resist the officers, whereupon Richardson covered him with a gun and when Douglass made a pass as if to resist, Richardson opened fire upon him, one bullet entering the left shoulder and passed out through the arm. Chas. Andrews, a negro bystander, says Richardson began shooting before resistance was made. Douglass is not known to have carried a weapon, though he was not searched.

The physician in attendance upon Douglass says his injury will not prove fatal.

SHERIFF OF SALUDA IS CHARGED WITH MURDER
He or Another Is Declared to Have Shot a Negro at the County Seat.
Columbia, S. C., Sept. 9.—On last Saturday night in the county of Saluda, at the county seat, those who ran out of their places of business upon hearing several pistol shots found the body of Bob Church, a negro, lying near the corner of Main and Church streets. There was a bullet hole through his head, and in a few moments the negro breathed his last. There was no one in sight.

A great sensation was created on Monday evening when the coroner's jury, which had been in secret session since the occurrence, adjourned and the coroner, without intimating to any one the nature of the verdict, walked across the street, and going into a store, laid his hand upon the arm of W. Lee Rhoden, the sheriff of Saluda county, and informed him that he was under arrest upon the charge of murder. The coroner took him to the sheriff's office and still has him in custody.

Having arrested the sheriff the coroner let it be known that he also wanted Matt W. Berry, a young man who
bob-crouch-saluda-1903-09-05.A2:
resided about eight miles from the town. Berry had been in town the day of the crime and had left the morning after. Hearing that he was wanted he went to the county seat and surrendered himself.

It now transpires that the coroner's jury rendered a verdict charging the sheriff and Berry with the crime upon the testimony of Hope Coleman and John Jeter, negroes, who swore that the fatal shot was fired by Berry or Rhoden, they could not tell which. Coleman also swore that he heard Berry tell Rhoden a few minutes before the shooting that he intended to kill a man, and Rhoden promised to help him. None of the white men who were near the scene of the crime could tell who fired the shot.

This is the first time in many years that a county sheriff has been arrested upon such a charge in South Carolina. It is noteworthy that Saluda county is a part of the original Edgefield county and is the county for the formation of which the late George D. Tillman made such a strenuous fight in the constitutional convention of 1895, an incident of which was the bitter fight over the naming of the county, during which "Uncle George" and Ben Tillman had their personal passage at arms.

The affair was a complete surprise and soon a large crowd had gathered around the dying man. During the afternoon and even after sundown there were a number of negroes on the streets, but there was no disturbance of any kind.

Immediately after the negro died Coroner Gipson summoned a jury of inquest and proceeded to take the testimony of several negroes who had been arrested and lodged in jail as probable witnesses. At 1 o'clock the inquest was adjourned until Sunday morning. The eye witnesses Saturday night placed the Crouch negro almost in the middle of Main street, where it is intersected by Church street, when the shot was fired, and standing alone. Pope Coleman had just left him and was walking away looking back over his right shoulder, still talking with Bob, when a shot, coming, as he stated, from the side of the brick building, was fired and the negro fell. He saw two men at the place where the pistol shot came from, but did not state who they were until recalled Sunday morning. In his testimony he says he was afraid to tell Saturday night what he knew; was afraid he'd be killed, and then goes on to say that the two men he saw were Sheriff Rhoden and Mr. Matt Berry. He states that he is positive, having passed them near this place just before the shooting and having also recognized them when his attention was attracted by the pistol shot.

Another negro practically corroberates Pope Coleman's testimony, after stating this morning that he, too, was afraid to tell what he knew about the affair.

Sheriff Of Saluda Arrested.
A Mysterious Murder with Which He is Charged by the Coroner's Jury—Very Unusual Case.
Special to The State.
Saluda, Sept. 7. — Saturday just after dark a pistol shot disturbed the usual quietude of our town and the body of Bob Crouch, colored, was found lying in the street, near the corner of Main and Church streets; a bullet hole was found running from the right to the left side of his head, just over the ear. The negro was alive when found but was unconscious and died in a short while.

An investigation as to the cause of his death was begun immediately and every one who had been known to be in the vicinity was questioned; a number of negroes were placed in jail, but no one seemed to know who fired the pistol.

Coroner Gibson took charge of the matter and began the inquest at once.

Pope Coleman, Poyton Graham, Luke Moore and Martin Bennett, all negroes, and Mr. W. H, Crawford, a young merchant, were examined that night, but the place from where the shot came could not be located, the witnesses differing, and none swore he knew the man who fired the shot. Coleman swore two white men did it from the corner of Smith Bros'. store, but said he did not know them.

The inquest was adjourned until Sunday morning. Rumors of all kinds were afloat and various opinions were afloat, but nothing definite could be learned.

Sunday morning the coroner decided to continue the inquest in secret and no one was admitted to the room save jurors, clerk and witnesses.

For four hours witnesses were examined. Then the coroner and jurors quietly came out of the room. No one said anything. The verdict of the jury was kept secret for a few minutes until Coroner Gibson walked over to Dowling's drug store, near the room where the inquest was held and close to the place where Crouch was shot, laid his hand on the arm of W. Lee Rhoden, Sheriff of Saluda county, and informed him of his arrest on the charge of murdering Crouch. The sheriff coolly and deliberately walked with the coroner to the sheriff's office and Coroner Gibson still has him in charge.

It was rumored that another white man was implicated and in a short time it leaked out that Matt W. Berry, a young man who resides about eight mile from here, was the person.

Berry had been in town Saturday night and Sunday morning; he was a witness at the inquest. After his examination he went to his home. This morning he came to Saluda and surrendered himself, having learned that the inquest jury had charged him with Crouch's murder.

The testimony on which the verdict implicating Rhoden and Berry was found came from Pope Coleman and John Jeter, negroes, who both swore that the shot was fired by either Rhoden or Berry (he didn't know which it was). Coleman also swore that he heard Berry tell Rhoden a few minutes

None of the white men who were in the neighborhood of the shooting could say who did the shooting. Several other negroes who were around could or would not tell and some of them apparently were nearer the firing party than either Jeter or Coleman.

Rhoden and Berry were both present at the inquest Saturday night.

Everything is quiet; everybody is anxious to know the truth of the matter; few opinions are being expressed openly, but those that are expressed are to the effect that the men implicated are innocent.

Reckless Sheriff Rhoden.
Not only Refused to Allow the Coroner Take his Place, but Refused to be Locked Up in Jail and Discharged the Jailer.
Special to News and Courier.
Special to News and Courier.

Columbia, Sept. 18.—Governer Heyward received the following letter this afternoon from Mr. Jacob Gibson, coroner of Saluda County:

Saluda, S. C., September 16, 1903.

Governor D, C. Heyward, Columbia, S. C—Dear Sir: Last week I officially notified you by wire that the sheriff of this county was under arrest, charged with the crime of murder, and that he refused to turn over his office to me as coroner, and asked for directions.

I received your reply that you had not been officially notified and that nothing was in your office for you to act on.

I now make official notification of the affairs. On Saturday night, September 5, 1903, Robert Crane, a negro, was shot on the public street in the town of Saluda, and after inquisition by me as coroner the jury returned a verdict that the negro came to his death by a gunshot wound in the hands of W. L. Rhoden and Mat Berry, whereupon I caused the said Rhoden and Berry to be arrested and committed them to custody.

In pursuance to the law I demanded that the office of sheriff be turned over to me, but the sheriff refused, and ordered me from the jail, where he refused to be locked up, and discharged his jailer, who is my son, and appointed another jailer, from whom I took a receipt for the two prisoners.

The jailer has moved out of the jail and there is no one legally in charge of affairs of that office. The sheriff has since been released from custody under habeas corpus proceedings and still continues to discharge the dutes of sheriff, which, in my opinion, is contrary to the law. I wish that you would advise me in the premises, as I have a prisoner that must be delivered and put in custody. Your prompt attention will oblige.

Jacob Gibson, Coroner, &c.

This is, perhaps, the first case of its kind in the history of the State, and as there was no precedent of guide Governor Heyward turned the whole matter over to Attorney General Gunter. Until an opinion is rendered in the case Governor Heyward can do nothing.

Thought to Have Been Result of Negro Preacher's Declaration.
(By Associated Press.)

CHICAGO, ILL., May 15.—Another church was wrecked by dynamite to-night, when a bomb was exploded under the pulpit of the African Methodist Church at Evanston. The interior was demolished and the front of the building blown out.

Two motives are ascribed for the demolishing of the building. The first is that certain colored people were incensed by a sermon preached last week by the pastor, Rev. I. N. Daniels, who said this was the white man's country, and the colored man might as well make up his mind to it now and get along the best he could. The other is that the members were incensed at the position taken by the pastor and a guest from Chicago, who had spoken against policy.

Chicago Pastor Had Severely Criticised His Race.

The crusade began in Chicago against policy playing and which spread to the North Shore suburb Thursday night is ascribed by a part of the congregation as the motive. The pastor told his flock that there were too few real men and women among the negroes; that this is the white man's country, and that unless the negro soon comes to an understanding of this and follows in his footsteps, instead of attempting to rule, there is little hope for the race.

Belleville, Ill., June 8. — County School Superintendent Charles Hertel, of St. Clair county, was shot and mortally wounded in his office here by W. T. Wyatt, a colored school teacher of East St. Louis, whose certificate to teach he had refused to renew. Wyatt was immediately arrested and taken to jail. Two hours later a mob stormed the jail, secured Wyatt, and despite the appeals of the mayor and other officials Wyatt was hanged with short ceremony. Superintendent Hertel was removed to the hospital, where the physicians probed for the bullet, but they state that there is no chance for his recovery. Hertel was aroused sufficiently to tell that Wyatt had shot him because of his refusal to renew the certificate.

Mob Forces the Jail.

A young man named Fielder was in the office when the shooting occurred. He grappled with Wyatt, but the negro beat him off with the butt of his revolver, inflicting a severe scalp wound. A passing policeman hurried into the room and succeeded in arresting the negro. He was taken to the county jail and the place was surrounded with policemen, as it was feared that a mob might form. A couple of hours passed when suddenly a mob appeared before the jail and forced a passage to Wyatt's cell. Securing the prisoner they dragged him out and hanged him. Before being executed Wyatt asserted the shooting was the result of a political grudge—that is, that Hertel refused to renew Wyatt's certificate because Wyatt had offended Hertel politically.

Eager to Torture the Victim.

The mob hanged Wyatt to a telephone pole in the public square. Even while his body was jerking in the throes of death from strangulation members of the mob began building a fire at the foot of the pole. The flames flared up and licked at the feet of the victim, but this did not satisfy the mob, and another and larger fire was started nearby. When it had begun burning briskly the negro, still half alive, was cut down, and after being covered with coal oil he was cast into the fire.

Moans Came from the Pyre.

Moans of pain were heard from the half dead victim of the mob and these served to further infuriate his torturers. They fell upon him with clubs and knives and cut and beat the burning body almost to pieces, and not until every sign of life had departed did they desist and permit the flames to devour the body. As the fire lighted up the scene the members of the mob stood around the funeral pyre hurling more faggots of wood in the flames and denouncing the negro for the shooting. After the body had been reduced to ashes the mob departed and all became quiet.

dennis-head-chinquepin-1903-07-16.A13:
TWO NEGROES PAY THE DEATH PENALTY
FURTHER DETAILS OF THE MURDER NEAR BATESBURG
Killing of Postmaster at Chinquapin Followed By Two Lynchings—Accounts Are Conflicting.
News and Courier.
Aiken, July 18.—Reports reached Aiken on Thursday of the murder of Mr. William Hall, postmaster at Chinquapin postoffice, near the line between Aiken and Lexington counties, by George Edwards, a negro; also the killing of two negroes by white men in search of Edwards. Chinquapin is in Aiken county, twenty-five miles from this city, and has no telephone or telegraph communication with the outside world.

Mr William Hall was a prominent young man of about 33 years of age and a scion of a peaceful, law-abiding family of some prominence in the community.

About a year ago Mr. Hall had a dispute with Edwards about an account Edwards owed him. Edwards refused to pay the bill and Mr. Hall ordered him off his premises and told him not to put his foot on the place again. Edwards threatened then to kill Mr. Hall, but no attention was paid to the matter, as his threats were thought to be only the bluster of a bully. Several times after that Mr. Hall bore the insults of the negro.

On Wednesday the negro came into Mr. Hall's store and offered to sell some tobacco tags. The negro had a gun with him and Mr. Hall asked him what he was doing with it. Edwards replied that he was just carrying it to do a little shooting. Mr. Hall told him that he knew he was carrying that gun to kill him with, and told Edwards that he was tired of his insolence and that he had better look out or he would thrash him.

The negro walked out of the store and went to his house across the creek, in Lexington county. As he went across the bridge he fired his gun, and when Mr. Hall heard this token of defiance he told his twenty-year old brother, Judson, to go to the house and get their guns, and they would go to Edward's house and give him the thrashing that was promised. The two Halls came upon the negro in his house and William, telling Judson to hold his gun on Edwards, proceeded to give the negro the lash. A negro woman in the house, thinking the white men intended to kill Edwards, threw herself between him and the white men. Edwards reached around the woman while she was arguing with the Halls and grabbed the gun out of William's hand and shot him through the heart. He then dragged Judson out of the house and beat him up very badly in the face and breast and would, no doubt, have killed him if he had not been stopped by the woman.

Magistrate Shealey, of Lexington county, held an inquest over William Hall on Thursday morning, and the jury brought in the usual verdict, viz: William Hall was killed by a gunshot wound at the hands of George Edwards.

A party searching for Edwards on Thursday, about 1 a.m., went to the house of Dennis Head, in Aiken county, a known pal of the negro, and, upon being refused admittance, broke open the door and pulled out Head and a negro boy and told them that if they would keep quiet they would not be hurt. Head was bound to prevent treachery and placed in a buggy. While the party was searching the house Head asked them to let the boy bring his clothes from the house. The men allowed the boy to do this and when he brought out the bundle they told him to toss it to Head in the buggy. When the boy threw it the bundle struck the wheel of the vehicle and a pistol fell out of it. When the boy saw that his plan was discovered he drew a revolver and fired pointblank at one of the white men. The men shot him to pieces and also killed Head.
dennis-head-chinquepin-1903-07-16.A16:
SLAIN BY A MOB.
Citizens Lynch the Man in Whose Yard Hall Was Killed.
A SEQUEL OF THAT MURDER.
Head Was in Conspiracy to Murder Hall. Details of the Latest Appeal to Judge Lynch.
Lynch.

The Batesburg correspondent of The State says just across the line in Aiken county Willie Hall was buried Thursday morning in Mountable churchyard. Not two miles away lies the dead body of Dennis Head, a negro, shot to death in sight of his home. Your correspondent visited the scenes of the recent tragedies Friday, going first to the home of Dennis Head, colored, where the Hall murder was committed. The house, a tiny log cabin, stands on a hill in the middle of a cornfield, and in the door, gazing out into the west, sat an old negro woman, wizened in years, the mother of Denn's Head. Near her on a bench was an aged man, her husband. He is so old that he sits in a half stupor and cannot answer any questions put to him. Elsie Head, the sister of Dennis Head, a negro girl of about 25 years, told The State representative Friday of the killing of Willie Hall, giving in substance the same account as already printed in The State.

THE MURDER OF HALL.

It seems that George Edwards, a negro came into the store of the Halls on Wednesday afternoon and asked Willie Hall to exchange some tobacco tags which he had for a small present of some kind. There had been feeling between the negro and Hall for some time on account of a previous dispute concerning a purchase in the store. The negro carried a shotgun and looking at it, Hall said: "You have got that gun for me." The negro made some surly reply and going out of the store halted on the bridge and fired a shot in the air. He then left the scene, going to the home of Dennis Head, in Lexington county, about three-quarters of a mile away. Not long afterwards, so Judson Hall himself told your correspondent Friday, he and his brother loaded their shotguns and followed the negro intenders with him and teach him a lesson. Arriving at the home of Dennis Head they found Edwards seated just inside the door. Both men leveled the irguns at him, and, as they entered the house, Elsie Head rushed past and out of the door. Edwards seized Will Hall's gun by the muzzle and a terrific struggle ensued in which the negro captured the weapon, and turning, shot his assailant through the abdomen. The wounded man cried: "I am shot," and half fell, half walked down the steps into the yard, where he expired in a few minutes. Edwards rushed at Judson Hall, the younger brother, and tried to wrest his shotgun from him, but Elsie Head assisted the white man in the struggle and finally the negro looked Hall in the eye and said: "Let me go; I won't shoot you." Judson Hall took the gun, and, examining it, said it was not loaded, so he says. In some way Edwards gained possession of it and ran across the fields unmolested because his opponent was physically exhausted.

The coroner was summoned and viewed the body of Hall, but the inquest was not held until Friday morning, when a verdict was rendered saying that Edwards had committed the crime. The same afternoon Butler Fox, a resident of Batesburg, bought a number of shotgun shells and some rifles in the town, saying that his "partner" had been killed, and that other men were in danger.

DENNIS HEAD KILLED.

Soon after the moon rose the same night Dennis Head, a negro living in Aiken perhaps a mile and a half across the county line, was called to his door by a number of white men who asked for a drink of water. As he opened the door one of the men clutched him by the wrist saying: "You are under arrest," and carrying him into the road a few hundred yards away. His wife tells the rest of the story, for strange though it may seem, no one else could be found who could or would tell anything about Head's killing. Jesse Butler, a negro of 18 years, went with Head into the road, says his wife, but soon ran back crying that he had been cruelly beaten. Shots were heard immediately afterwards and the men left the scene. One of the women ran out into the road and stumbled over the body of Head. She threw her arms around his neck and he muttered some incoherent phrase. The woman was terrified by the crime and ran away leaving the dying man. His body was not removed until Thursday morning, and Friday afternoon it was lying on the porch of the cabin covered by a sheet and shielded from the sun by a few quilts hung on a chair. A negro sat near and waved a leafy bough to keep away the incessant swarm of flies, the while crooning a plaintive song. The man was shot through the left side of the stomach and must have died in agony. Clara Head, his wife, said that Butler believed that there were three men in the party and that Head was tied while they were whipping the smaller boy. In the road lay a harness strap tied into a knot, the negro's hat, buggy whip broken to pieces, and a shot gun shell from a 12-bore gun. Head's body was still lying on his porch Friday night,

Thursday about 1 a.m. a posse in search of George Edwards went to the house of Dennis Head, in Aiken county, a known pal of Edwards, and, upon being refused admittance, broke open the door and dragged out Dennis and a negro boy about 18 years of age. The negroes were told that no harm was intended and if they would keep quiet the white men would search the house and leave them alone. dennis-head-chinquepin-1903-07-16.A21:
Murder In Lexington and Aiken.
Batesburg special of Friday to Charlotte Observer: As the result of trouble with a Negro customer, Will Hall, a merchant of Aiken county, was killed by George Edwards. In the search for the latter two other Negroes were arrested. They made a break for liberty and one was killed, the other getting away. Will Hall was a merchant who kept a country store at Chinquepin, in Aiken county, eight miles southeast of this place. Yesterday at noon George Edwards, colored, went to his store with some tobacco tags for sale. The Negro had a gun with him and it seems that Hall and the Negro had some words, after which the latter left and fired off his gun not far from the store. Hall then closed up his store and went to his brother's, who lived a short distance away. They armed themselves with breech-loading guns and followed Edwards about a mile and a half over into Lexington county to the home of Lewis Cullum, a Negro nearly 100 years old. At this place they found Edwards. As the Hall brothers went into the house a Negro woman got between them and Edwards. At this juncture Edwards grabbed Hall's gun and wrenched it from him and shot him through the heart, killing him instantly. The Negro then sprang like an enraged animal on the younger brother, Judson Hall, and would have killed him had it not been for the pleading of the woman. Edwards then walked off, carrying one of the guns with him. The news of the homicide spread like wildfire and by night the lonely country in which the tragedy was enacted looked like a camp of soldiers, people of the surrounding country and from a distance being there in large numbers. In their search for Edwards they went to the home of Dennis Head, who lives on the Alken county side, about two miles from the scene of the crime. It seems that Edwards was seen to go into his house late in the afternoon and upon questioning Dennis he became highly incensed. It is said that he and a Negro named Jesse Butler were tied and on being marched back to the main crowd they made a break for liberty. At this juncture Dennis was shot and died instantly. Several shots were fired at Butler, but they went wild of the mark and he escaped. Why Head was killed and Butler shot at has not been satisfactorily explained. Hall was a young, unmarried man and had property and friends in the vicinity, in which he lived, and his death is much deplored. The coroner's jury rendered a verdict that Hall came to his death by a gun-shot wound in the hands of George Edwards. Edwards is still at large, but parties are looking for him.

dennis-head-chinquepin-1903-07-16.A34:
A Reward Offered.
Governor Offers $500 For Ar-
Rest of Lynchers—Lawless-
ness In Aiken County
Condemned—What
the Governor
says of the
Matter.
Columbia Record.
Governor Heyward has offered a reward of $500 for the apprehension and conviction of the Aiken county lynchers, who recently killed Dennis Head. In discussing the matter said:

"The recent killing of Dennis Head by a mob in Aiken county is the climax of a spirit of lawlessness which means danger and disgrace to South Carolina. I shall administer to the perpetrators of such an inhuman outrage as stern a rebuke and as condign punishment as are afforded by the laws of the state of South Carolina. I fully realize that nothing can be done until the identity of the slayers has been revealed. That those who committed such a deed keep in the dark is self acknowledged guilt. Every aid that the law affords to apprehend and punish the guilty parties will be invoked and I shall do my utmost to see that the law is vindicated. In order to further this to the very best of my ability and for the additional reason that a determined effort shall be made and kept up I have offered a reward of $500 for the apprehension and conviction of the parties who committed this deed.

"I have written to Solicitor Davis informing him of the situation as I have gathered it from the newspapers. I regret to say that, though I have waited several days for official notice regarding this lawless act, not one report has reached me, through the officers of the law. I am very indignant about this killing. There seems to have been no reason whatever for such a crime and the action of the guilty parties is entirely indefensible."
dennis-head-chinquepin-1903-07-16.A42:
$1,500 in Rewards.

NEGROES BARELY ESCAPE ANGRY MOB
ED HUTCHESON AND HIS WIFE AT SCOTTSBORO CAUSE INDIGNA TION BY WRITING OBSCENE LETTER TO YOUNG LADY.
Scottsboro, July 20. — (Special.) — Ed Hutcheson, a negro, together with his wife, Rosa, was arrested at Stevenson late yesterday afternoon and brought to Scottsboro on the midnight train on the charge of writing an obscene letter to Miss Foster, the young daughter of Thomas Foster, ex-tax assessor, and one of the most prominent men in the county. It was known that these negroes wrote the letter and signed the name of John Rice, another negro, to get revenge. This, it is said, so infuriated a number of the citizens of Stevenson that it was feared a mob would take the negroes and lynch them.

Sheriff Austin and Solicitor Proctor were at once notified by telephone of the condition of affairs. The sheriff immediately instructed the officer that had the negroes to get them away at once, and the officer brought them to Scottsboro. About fifty men were closing around them as they were hustled aboard the train at Stevenson. The sheriff took charge of the negroes and put them in jail at once and heavily armed the guards on duty.

Sheriff Austin and Solicitor Proctor went to Stevenson this morning to investigate more fully. Considerable indignation is felt over the insulting letter mailed to the young lady by these negroes. It is thought good counsel will prevail and a lynching be averted.

SCOTTSBORO.
Negro Who Sent Obscene Letters By Mail Will Be Saved From Mob.
Scottsboro, July 21.—(Special.) — Ed Hutcherson and his wife, Rosa, the negroes that were arrested at Stevenson on the charge of sending obscene letters to a young lady at that place, and who just escaped lynching at the hands of infuriated citizens, are safely in jail here and will have a preliminary trial Monday next before Judbe C. The people, while greatly incensed, are disposed to await the action of the courts. However, guards are still at the jail as a precaution.

Strauss Edmonds and Miss Minnie Welsh were quietly married at Paint Rock last Sunday night, Mayor Green officiating.

Capt. William Glover, an old and highly eesteemed citizen of this county, died at his home in Bridgeport Monday morning at an early hour, aged about 80 years. Joseph M. SCOTTSBORO.
Negroes Are Sentenced for Writing Obscene Letters.
Scottsboro, July 29.—(Special.)—in the trial here yesterday before C. L. Cargill, judge of probate, Ed Hutchinson and his wife, Rosa, were fined $500 and sentenced to six months' hard labor for the county. They are the negroes that were arrested and narrowly escaped a lynching at Stevenson a few days ago. The charge against them was writing obscene letters to Miss Foster, daughter of ex-Tax Assessor Tom Foster of Stevenson.

While waiting for the train that was to convey them to the penitentiary the woman, Rosa, who had her infant in her arms, managed to elude the guard, slipped off in the darkness, and made her escape. Sheriff Austin this morning offered a reward of $10 for her capture.

Blackwell Hewlett, son of Capt. and Mrs. T. H. Hewlett, who died here yesterday, will be buried today. Rev. W. T. Blackwell, assisted by Rev. S. J Parrish, will conduct the funeral obsequies.

SCOTTSBORO.
Negro Woman Who Escaped Recaptured—Mob After Rapist.
Word was received here today that a white man named Mark Kelly assaulted the little twelve-year-old daughter of Robert West, who lives on Cumberland mountain in this county. Kelly was arrested by constable Flippo and while waiting for a preliminary hearing made his escape. A number of infurated citizens are hot after him. His father lives in Franklin county, Tennessee, and it is thought he is making for that point.

Rosa Hutchinson, the negro woman convicted before Judge C. L. Corgill yesterday on two charges of writing obscene letter and who escaped from jail last Tuesday night, was captured near Sturmon today. Perry Pipps brought his bloodhounds down from Chattanooga, and they were well on the trail of the woman when a message was received that Constable Darwin had effected her capture. She had made the trip to Bars, a distance of 25 miles, in one night with a baby in her arms.

FIENDISH Was the Murder of Mrs. Alice Matthews. HACKED TO PIECES WITH AX AFTER SHE HAD BEEN CRIMINALLY ASSAULTED. LITTLE DAUGHTER MANGLED. Negro Against Whom Evidence Was Strong Shot To Death While Running Away. ONCE LIVED IN LOUISVILLE. Shreveport, La., April 11.—[Special.] —Mrs. Alice Matthews, aged forty-five years, wife of Frank Matthews, a well-known engineer, was brutally murdered in her bed early this morning by a negro who, it is believed, outraged his victim before slaying her. The woman's little daughter Aline, aged ten, was probably fatally wounded. An ax was the instrument employed in both cases. Ed Porter, a negro strongly suspected of the crime, was shot to death by two police sergeants while attempting to escape. He had been run down at a point about five miles from Shreveport. Discovery of the Crime.
The discovery of the crime was made at 5:30 o'clock this morning by a servant who entered the bedroom of Mrs. Matthews. The unfortunate woman, who was almost hacked to pieces, had been dead for some time. Her daughter was still alive when the servant entered. Entrance was effected through a side window, and although there were fifteen persons in the house, which is situated in the very heart of the residence district of Shreveport, no one heard a single suspicious sound during the night.

Had Been Assaulted.

The skull of Mrs. Matthews was crushed and she bore evidence of having been criminally assaulted. The child's skull was fractured, her chest crushed and shoulder lacerated. Mrs. Matthews wore a diamond ring and diamond earrings, which were not touched by the murderer, and three pocketbooks containing money were in the room, showing that criminal assault furnished the motive for the crime. An ax covered with blood and hair was found in the kitchen.

Negro Shot To Death.

Bloodhounds took up the trail of the murderer, but lost it after going a short distance. A Kansas City Southern engineer notified the police of the appearance of a negro covered with blood on the tracks of the railroad and a posse was organized to hunt him down. The posse separated and Sergeants Gerald and Roquemore soon came upon the negro. He made a desperate dash for a ravine and the officers fired four shots at him, two of which took effect in his back, killing him instantly. The negro's clothing was covered with blood and his shoes fitted the bloody footprints in the kitchen of the Matthews home. His name was Ed Porter, and he was a well-known Shreveport negro.

Came From Louisville.

Mrs. Alice Matthews, the victim of the murder and outrage, resided upwards of five years in Shreveport, coming here from Louisville. She was a Miss Hicks, of Somerset, Ky. A brother, Robert Hicks, resides at Birmingham, Ala., and a telegram was sent to him, telling of his sister's murder, with the request that he break the news to the woman's husband, who has a run as engineer out of Anniston, Ala., over the Seaboard Airline. Mrs. Matthews was held in the highest esteem here and her tragic death was a terrible shock to friends and acquaintances. The little girl is still alive, with a remote chance of recovery. Later to-day the child was operated on and a piece of the skull removed.

REPUBLICAN BOLT IN OMAHA CONVENTION.

Seventy-One Delegates Will Not Stand For Mayor Moores' Third Term Nomination.

Omaha, Neb., April 11—The Republicans to-day nominated Mayor Moores for re-election, and thereby precipitated a bolt of seventy-one delegates, who say that they will nominate a ticket of their own on Monday. The convention was so uproarious that the police were called in twice to quell the obstreperous delegates.

Mayor Moores was nominated for a third term on the first ballot by one vote. After eight wards had been called and voted, Chairman Goss, of the Ninth ward, demanded a poll of the Second ward. The chairman ignored him and ordered the secretary to proceed with the roll call. The convention was soon in an uproar, the police flocked on to the floor to preserve order, and forcibly pushed a number of the delegates into their seats. Those opposed to Moores' men said the chairman was arbitrary in his ruling, and when the chairman declared Moores nominated seventy-one delegates bolted. After the withdrawal of these delegates the remainder of the ticket was nominated by the regular convention.

Labor Troubles Over.

Labor Troubles Over. Cannelton, Ind., April 11.—[Special.]— The labor troubles which have existed during the past two years at the mines of the American Cannel Coal Company here have been amicably settled, and

the old men who were formerly employed are expected to return to their places in the mines next Tuesday. This will add to coal shipments on the Ohio.

JOHN H. PUNCH DIES
AT MT. STERLING.

Had Served For Several Years As Deputy Warden of the Frankfort Penitentiary.

Mt. Sterling, Ky., April 11.—[Special.]
—John Henry Punch, De puty Warden of the penitentiary at Frankfort, died at his home in this city to-day at 5 o'clock p. m. The funeral services will be held at St. Patrick's church, this city, Tuesday morning at 10 o'clock and the interment will be at Mt. Sterling.

Mr. Punch was thirty-one years old and left a wife and one child, a son four and one-half years old. He was a son of the late Capt. Patrick Punch, who had held various places of public trust and was United States Deputy Marshal under Capt. James Blackburn, John Henry Punch was a merchant here until he accepted the position of Deputy Warden under Col. Eph Lillard, succeeding the late Edward McGrath.

OFFICERS OF GEORGIA
BANK INDICTED.

President and Vice President of Warrenton Bank Charged With Wrecking the Concern.

Washington, Ga., April 11.—The grand jury of Warren county to-day returned indictments against W. S. Witham, of Atlanta, former president and financial agent, and E. B. Farmer, vice president of the bank at Warrenton, which institution closed its doors in February, 1902, owing to depositors some $16,000. The indictments charged felony in rendering the bank insolvent and loaning more than 10 per cent. of the capital stock to one officer of the bank.

MOB AFTER NEGRO

WHO STRUCK WHITE MAN AT INDIANAPOLIS.

Race War Would Have Followed,
But For Interference of Police
With Revolvers.

Indianapolis, April 11.—A fight between two white men and a negro at 5:30 o'clock this evening precipitated a race riot and the negro, Clifford Ball, a lad about twenty years old, narrowly escaped violence at the hands of a mob of a hundred men.

After striking one of the men, John Bush, on the head with a brick, knocking him senseless to the sidewalk, Ball ran south, pursued by half a dozen men. The crowd increased to a hundred, and cries of "lynch him" were heard as the mob pursued the flying negro through the streets. Policemen with drawn revolvers saved him.

EARTHQUAKE SHOCK
IN CITY OF MEXICO.

People Rushed Into the Streets In
Fright, But No Serious Damage
Is Reported.

Mexico City, April 11.—At 9:15 p. m. a sharp earthquake shock was felt in this city. Some excitement prevailed for a time, many people rushing into the street, fearing that the earthquake might prove serious. No damage resulted, however. It is not known whether the shock was felt in other portions of the republic.

IMPROVEMENT IN PLAGUE SITUATION.

Mazatlan, Mex., April 11.—There are now but two patients at the lazaretto, both of whom are rapidly improving. One man has died of the plague at the lazaretto at Siquieros. All other patients at that place are making quick recoveries.

port of the horrible tragedy which was enacted at the Matthews' home in this city, the truth when told, or the facts when narrated as obtained, are sufficiently sensational, blood-curdling and abhorrent without the indulgence in exaggerations or gruesome embellishment.

The excitement having been followed by the cool, sober sense of realization, the mind in a review of the dark picture of reality is led to inquire into the degree of satisfaction which may be derived from the cremation of a lifeless body.

It is true that the sheriff, the mayor and the chief of police had the body of the supposed murderer moved beyond the reach of those who clamored for it, and they did not anticipate its removal from the cemetery to the Levee, and therefore they must be held blameless for the action of the mob, who, in cremating a dead body, removed an important link in connection with a tragedy which appears to be shrouded in the deepest mystery. It was a mistake! A serious mistake.

THE CORONER'S INQUEST.

It is due Dr. Coty, coroner, to say that he contributed his best effort and long experience in trying to unravel the horrible crime, and to assist him he had as jurors five gentlemen, Zach Howel, J. nett and H. A. Fetzer, who rank with H. Prescott, James Keeney, Albert Barthe best and most reliable of the community, men of judgment, conscientious, conservative, fair and impartial men. It could not be possible to have obtained a better jury. These gentlemen deliberated long and earnestly, and on Sunday afternoon they reached the conclusion that Mrs. Alice Matthews had died from wounds inflicted by a person unknown to them and urged a thorough investigation by the grand jury. This conclusion is remarkable and is doubtless without a precedent in Caddo parish and is striking in the face of the sensational reports given in public print and in the face of the fact that a man claimed to have been the murderer had been shot and killed. The doubt of the jury is significant and still more direct when they urge a thorough investigation by the grand jury.

WAS AN INNOCENT MAN KILLED AND CREMATED?

The horror of Saturday is intensified by the report that the man shot and killed Saturday afternoon and whose body was burned on a pyre after midnight Saturday had no connection whatever with the murder of Mrs. Matthews. On the authority of Mr. Cal Vance and Mr. Stinson, most reputable and reliable citizens of Bossier, it appears that Albert Washington, the negro killed, was innocent. Both of these gentlemen stated positively and without reservation that Albert Washington worked on their place all day Friday; that he was on their plantation Friday night and Saturday morning; that he, with some other negroes, got on the Cotton Belt train at 10 o'clock Saturday morning, and that after reaching Shreveport on this train Saturday, he went to the hospital, where he expected to find his wife who had been sick, and on being told she had gone to DeSota parish, he announced that he would walk over to see her, and bidding his companions goodbye, he started on his journey. It was while journeying to DeSoto that he got on the Kansas City Southern track, and it was while he was in a cut on the K. C. S. road that he was halted by the police, and running away instead of stopping, was shot and killed. Both Mr. Vance and Mr. Stinson stated that several of the negroes working on the plantation and who were in this city on hearing that a dead negro had been taken to Willis's, the undertaker, called there to see the body, and that these negroes identified the body as that of Albert Washington, who got on the train with them at about 10 o'clock and reached Shreveport with him on the same train that day. These statements are startling, but they are forceful with truth which can not and must not be minimized. THE STATEMENT DISCREDITED.

Monday afternoon when these state-
ed-porter-shreveport-1903-04-11.A19:
SENSATIONAL EXPERIENCE OF ONE DAY AND NIGHT IN SHREVEPORT
The Excitement a Reminder of the Lynching of Jones and Hill--A Shocking Discovery--Was an Innocent Man Killed and Cremated?
were under discussion certain officials whom it is unnecessary to name grinned sardonically and stamped almost at one breath the whole story with discredit, giving in words the assurance that the right man had been killed, and there could be no doubt about it. Against such conclusion it were senseless to reason, but as we have said and repeat, it is significant that the coroner's jury, comprising five as intelligent, prudent and conservative men as can be mustered for such duty in Caddo parish, not only hesitated but have called on the grand jury for a more thorough investigation? If these five men had believed that the man killed was the man who had committed the murder, would they not have reached their verdict accordingly?

UNDER WHAT CIRCUMSTANCES WAS THE MAN KILLED.

The man killed, Albert Washington, was in a railroad cut of the K. C. S. about five miles from Shreveport. He was walking briskly. He was carrying his coat. He no doubt had espied some of the policemen who were scattered in that vicinity. Under a mental strain he was easily intimidated, and when halted by the officers who confronted him, he became excited, and when asked about blood as alleged being on his person, he started on a run, pursued by the officers by whom he was shot and killed.

OFFICER SJUSTIFIED.

Under the circumstances the officers were justified in law and reason to shoot. It is to be regretted that they could not take him alive. The officers acting under authority of the law could not permit the escape of a man who they had every reason to believe, especially by his running away, was the man they were seeking. If under the same circumstances the negro had been met by a sheriff's posse and had ran away he would doubtless have been killed. Viewed therefore from every reasonable standpoint the officers are justified. Had they permitted this man to escape they would have been censurable. But to emphasize how easily and readily a negro may become intimidated and stampede under the strain of fear, it may be recalled that soon after Mr. Foster had been murdered a squad of armed men appeared in sight near Bossier City. In a stable was an old negro, who, on seeing the crowd, jumped out of the stable and ran away. When called to stop he only increased his speed. He was fired at and shot, and then taken to Schumpert's Sanitarium. He recovered and is attending to his functions as usual in Bossier. He had no connection whatever with the crime, but lost his senses and stampeded at the sight of the armed men. The sense of stampede is uncontrollable, and some brave men have been known to run away when stampeded.

BLOODY HAND AND FINGERS.

One of the strong points of the authorities in maintaining that Albert Washington was the murderer of Mrs. Matthews is that when shot and killed his finger nails and hand were bloody.

Can it be said positively that when this man was halted before he started to run away that his hand was bloody and that his clothes were bloody? But Mr. Vance and Mr. Stinson are confident that there was no blood on the hands or the clothes of this negro when he got on the train Saturday morning at 10 o'clock, and the negroes, his companions, give the same assurance. This is somewhat perplexing, but let reason be applied. Men familiar with blood and shots and wounds, men for instance who were soldiers during the days of the Confederacy, will concede from experience that when a man is shot, unless completely disabled or killed, that the first impulse is to throw the hand to the wound if it can be reached. When shot, this negro was running; he was shot in the back, one of the bullets striking below the skull a little toward the right of the neck. Did not this man throw his hand to the back of his neck, where shot, and when running and before he fell, and in putting his hand to this wound did not his hand and his fingers become bloody? Is it not probable that the blood trickling from the wounds down his back and
ed-porter-shreveport-1903-04-11.A20:
from his breast run into his pants, and did he not become more or less bloody from these shots? Blood when smeared on the hand would dry rapidly, and blood when dried during several hours could not have been scraped off with a knife. The man's coat was bloody, but this blood came from the wounds inflicted by the officers.

A SINGULAR FEATURE.

Alluding to this coat, it may be said that it was not Albert Washington's coat, but Ed Porter's, a negro well known in Bossier. When Albert Washington got on the train Saturday morning, by mistake he took and wore off Ed Porter's coat. This coat should then establish in some degree, if not altogether, Albert Washington's identity. In this coat, which was in Albedt Washington's possession when killed, there was an account in Ed Porter's name. It was for goods purchased by Porter from the Benton Mercantile Company. There was no piece or part of a ring found in this coat, but a piece of glass which belonged to Ed Porter and the same Ed Porter is alive in Bossier. This may be "a coincidence," as said an officer when his attention was directed to the coat, but there is another Ed Porter who may be a "coincidence." It will be recalled that an officer identified beyond a doubt the body as being that of Ed Porter of the Union Depot, but when so informed Mr. Keeney, one of the jurors of inquest, was not satisfied, so he went in quest of the Ed Porter of the Union Depot and found him alive and well attending to his business, and the negro expressed his surprise to learn that he had been connected with the case—did not know that he had been killed and cremated.

ANOTHER BLOOD THEORY.

On the report of several friends of the Caucasian it may be said that the blood visible on the shirt and pants of the negro at the time he was halted and killed by the police, was from his handling of meat at the slaughter house on his route down the railroad. It is stated and it is believed that can be substantiated by witnesses, that when passing by some held was needed to handle the beef, and the negro was called to assist, for which he was given a silver quarter of a dollar, which is in the possession of a gentleman who may produce it in time. It may be said that this was an unfortunate transaction for the negro, and it was, since it may have led, innocently, to his death.

IF AN INNOCENT MAN WAS KILLED WHO IS GUILTY?

This case with all its "coincidences" and perplexities and its startling features appears to be plain and clear when practical thinking and logical reasoning is applied to it.

If Albert Washington was the murderer, why did he loiter about and delay his escape when he had opportunity to walk not less than twenty miles from the time the deed was accomplished to the hour when he was shot and killed?

How could Albert Washington have been in Bossier, as stated by Mr. Vance and Mr. Stinson and others, and be at the place then and where the crime was committed?

His flight when called to stop is explained by the parallel of the old negro in Bossier who fled at the sight of the armed men and was shot. Again, is it not reasonable to suppose that he had discovered his mistake in taking the wrong coat, and that he thought the officers wanted him for stealing it?

There has been a mistake. As well admit it and go ahead on some clue and catch the guilty man. Every law-abiding citizen is concerned in this case, and there must be no rest, no cessation of activity and vigilance. Who is the guilty man?

RIDICULOUS THEORIES.

One of the ridiculous theories palmed off sensationally on an intelligent public is that the murderer got into Mrs. Matthews' room through a window facing on the street; that after accomplishing a heinous crime he went to this window with bloody fingers, changed his mind and then unlocked the door leading into the kitchen; then walked into the yard, secured the ax, retraced his steps to the victim's side, then killed her and almost killed her daughter; walked out a second time, threw away the ax and disappeared.

THE CORRECT THEORY.
ed-porter-shreveport-1903-04-11.A21:

The coroner's jury, which held an inquest over the body of Mrs. Alice Matthews who was recently murdered near Shreveport, and for which crime a negro was killed and then his body cremtaed, is of the opinion that the wrong man was killed and has asked that the matter be investigated by the grand jury. FOUGHT OFF NEGRO WITH HER HATPIN Miss Emory, of Mt. Vernon, Puts Up a Plucky and Successful Fight with What She Calls "Woman's Ideal Weapon."
Attacked by a negro in a lonesome strip of woods in Bronxville, Miss Elsie Emory, private secretary of ex-Genator Trace N. Mills, battled for fifteen minutes with her assailant and at last succeeded in driving him away. after stabbing him repeatedly with her hatpin.

Miss Emory was visiting a friend in Bronxville last Saturday night and started for her home in Mount Vernon about 415. The road leading to the trolley guns through a dense patch of woods for about two hundred yards. Miss Emory, who is an athletic girl and an expert swimmer and equestrienne, entered the woods without fear. When about half way through she was suddenly seized from behind by a strong pair of arms. She screamed, and her assailant released one of her arms to place his hand over her mouth. It was at this moment that the girl showed her presence of mind.

Weapon Is Effective.

As soon as she felt her arm free she pulled her hatpin from her bonnet and plunged it with all her strength into the thug's arm. The man uttered a cry of pain, but instead of releasing her he picked her up and attempted to carry her into the underbrush. Miss Emory jabbed the pin again and again into the brute's chest and neck. Unable to endure the pain any longer, the infuriated man dropped his burden and struck the girl two blows in the face; the second of which left her senseless and bleeding on the ground.

The negro, not waiting to see the result of his blows, dashed into the underbrush.

Miss Emory was at work as usual this morning, but her face was badly swollen and discolored. She said to an Evening World reporter:

"I do not wish to be made a heroine. I simply acted on impulse and did what any other girl would do under the circumstances, use the woman's ideal weapon, the hatpin."

Still Another Assault.

About two hours before Miss Emory was assaulted Mrs. Daniel Scott of No. 818 South Sixth avenue, Mount Vernon, who is private secretary to the firm of Peter Henderson & Company, seed merchants, was walking along Fourth avenue, Mount Vernon, when she felt a pair of arms circle her waist.

"Stop fooling, Dan," said Mrs. Scott, thinking it was her husband, but instead of her husband's voice came a rough demand for her purse. Mrs. Scott started to struggle, but the highwayman struck her a violent blow on the ear, telling her to the pavement, and grabbed her purse and disappeared. The police of both Mount Vernon and Yonkers are leaving no stone unturned to discover the man, but their efforts so far have been fruitless.

Chief Foley, of the Mount Vernon police, believes the assault to have been committed by the same man.

A negro was arrested last night on suspicion, but neither Miss Emory nor Mrs. Scott could identify him, and he was released. There have been a number of assaults in this district lately and many citizens talk of organizing a vigilance committee.

THEY FEARED LYNCHING.
Bronxville Police Removed Accused Negro to Mount Vernon.
I. N. MILLS'S SECRETARY ATTACKED
Locked up in Mount Vernon is "Ned" Green, the colored Berry Wall of that city, who was arrested yesterday, charged with assault in the first degree. The complainant is Miss Lillian Imrie, private secretary of ex-Senator Isaac N. Mills, of Mount Vernon. Feeling is running high against Green, whom Miss Imrie has identified as the man who held her up near the Old Dutch Reformed Church on Saturday evening. There are some Bronxville villagers who favored taking the law into their own hands and lynching Green.

Saturday night Miss Imrie was detained at her office in Mount Vernon until 8 o'clock. When she neared the Old Dutch Reformed Church a burly negro stepped out from behind a tree and seized her by the throat. Miss Imrie fought, but was unable to loosen his hold. She reached for her hatpin, and after being jabbed several times with it the negro let go. Then Miss Imrie yelled for help. The negro struck her several blows in the face, but Miss Imrie's cries were heard by Clarence Moore, of Bronx Manor, who ran to her alld. Then the negro disappeared.

Miss Imrie was assisted to her home, a short distance away, and the Bronxville and Mount Vernon police were informed. A vigilance committee was organized and they scoured the woods for the criminal.

Green's record in Mount Vernon is bad. Although he is only twenty-eight years old, he has been convicted fourteen times. He has also served time in the Kings County Penitentiary.

Green was arraigned before Judge Thatcher, in the parlor of Chief Van Buren's home at Bronxville, last night. He pleaded not guilty and was held in $2,000 bail.

The hearing was not public, as the Bronxville authorities feared an attempt might be made by the friends of Miss Imrie to attack Green. Green says he can prove an alibi. As it was feared that the Bronxville lockup was not a safe place to keep Green, he was committed to the Mount Vernon police station until his trial. Green, in trying to establish an alibi, told the police that he went to Port Chester on the day of the alleged assault to sell some tickets to James S. Merritt, who was on the Republican ticket for Sheriff. Green admitted, also, in order to exonerate himself, that he called on Mayor Fuske, the opponent of Mr. Merritt, on the same errand. He posed as a political leader.

MOUNT VERNON, Nov. 12.—Protesting his innocence and declaring that he will establish an alibi, Ned Green, called "the Berry Wall of Mount Vernon" because he has always been the smartest dressed negro in town, spent the night in a cell at Police Headquarters.

Fearing that some of the friends of Miss Tilden Imrie, the stenographer for ex-Senator Isaac N. Mills, who accuses Green of attacking her at Bronxville, might attempt to lynch Green, the authorities were afraid to look him up in the dingy little jail at Bronxville and so under orders of Judge Thatcher he was kept here.

Miss Imrie reiterates her statement that she is positive that Green is the man who seized her by the throat and tried to force her through the hedge near the Bronxville church the night before election.

She fought the man with her hat pin and tried to scratch his face. Her screams for help were heard by Clarence Moore and then her assailant ran away. A vigilance committee comprising residents of Bronxville searched the woods for several days, but could get no trace of the negro.

A hearing was given Green in the parlor of Chief of Police Van Buren's home, and Judge Thatcher, of Bronxville, today fixed Green's bail at $2,000 pending the examination to-morrow.

Senator Mills appeared before the Judge and said that in behalf of the District-Attorney he would prosecute Green. Stephen J. Stillwell, counsel for Green, declared that the prisoner would prove a clear alibi.

"Why, do you know," said Mr. Stillwell, "we have fifty witnesses to prove where Green was on the night of the alleged assault. In the first place, Green was interviewing the Republican candidate for Sheriff at Portchester at 5 o'clock on that night. It took him nearly an hour and a half to reach here. At 7.05 P. M. he was talking to Mayor Fiske, and from 7.30 until 9 he was at a Republican meeting, as we shall prove by Alderman Maxon."

Green says all his ill luck is due to a black cat.

"On the night before I was arrested," said he, "a black cat ran in front of me twice. I knew I was in for something then. I had a tip on Orthodox in the first race yesterday and would have made $100 if I had not been pinched."

Miss Imrie will prove by a conductor on a Huckleberry trolley car that he saw a man answering Green's description standing by the Bronxville Church, and he will identify him positively in court.

PERCY WHITE'S SLAYER CAUGHT IN MARYLAND
When Officers Arrested Him He Confessed to Firing Fatal Shot
Chester, Pa., Aug. 1.—Elias Williams, the negro murderer of Farmer Percy White, of Springfield township, Delaware county, was arrested yesterday on a farm near Cockeysville, Md., by Detectives Hogan and Dick, of the Baltimore force.

Williams confessed to the murder and told the whole story to Detective Berry, of Chester, who, with Deputy Sheriff Wolff, was summoned soon after the arrest had been made.

"When I shot Percy White," said Williams to Detective Berry, "I ran as hard as I could down the lane and out into the road. I knew they would be after me, and I threw away the gun because that would give me away if anybody saw me with it. I hid it in the bushes along the way, and as soon as it was dark I went to Chester.

"I was awful skeered that the cops would get me, 'cause I knew they would be looking for me; but there is so many negroes in Chester that an extra one don't count.

"I kept along the darkest streets I could find, and went to the Pennsylvania station on Sixth street, and took the train leaving at half past 11 for Baltimore.

"I have been staying in Baltimore all this time, and at last was working on a farm out at Cockeysville. I had to keep shady, 'cause I knew the police were on the lookout. I heard of your being down, and couldn't sleep for thinking of shooting young Percy.

"I don't know what made me do it, but the devil got in me, and while I was hot under the collar I got the gun and went there to kill him."

Media, Pa., Oct. 7.—Ellias Williams, the colored farmhand who was placed on trial here Monday charged with the killing of Percy White, the young Springfield farmer, on June 19 last, was convicted of murder in the second degree. BUNGALOOS ON WARPATH SEVERAL NEGROES CHASED THROUGH DOWNTOWN STREETS. Loud Words of Two Intoxicated Colored Men Started the Trouble Large Crowd Assembled.
For three hours last night the Bungaloos had control of the down-town streets and caused terror to many negroes that happened along. The trouble started about 8 o'clock and continued till 11 o'clock, when many fell by the wayside as the pace of running through alleys and over streets tired their bodies. Despite the number of police on duty on the down-town streets, ruffians ran wild, yelling, shouting and throwing missiles after fleeing negroes. From a crowd of twenty young boys that appeared at Illinois street at 8 o'clock thirsting for the blood of some Ethiopian, the crowd by 9 o'clock numbered nearly five hundred. Many of these did not take part in the assaults, but their presence and evident approbation of the work of the younger boys gave the latter courage.

The first uprising occurred at 8 o'clock, near the New Claypool Hotel, when two dark-skinned negroes passed the corner cursing and abusing many white men and women. Several of the white men upbraided the negroes for their conduct and in a short time a crowd gathered. The members of the Bungaloos were on a corner across the street, and when they saw the crowd their curiosity caused them to investigate. When they learned that two drunken negroes were responsible for the trouble their chief was not long in calling his men into action. Several squeaky voices yelling "Kill the niggers!" was the first incentive. The crowd turned and the negroes, seeing that delay might be dangerous, decided to leave. They started across Illinois street toward the south side, but were followed by the angry mob of whites. The procession, led by the two negroes, moved east on Washington street, when, scared by the mutterings of the leaders of the whites, the two negroes darted abruptly across Washington street and turned north into Meridian. The smaller of the negroes, frightened nearly to death by this time, lost his hat in his hurried flight across the street. Reaching the alley north of Washington street, he turned and beheld several hundred more whites who appeared eager to do harm. The smaller negro tugged once at the arm of his companion. This was for the two to disappear somewhere and they darted into the alley. They were chased to Illinois street, where they boarded a street car going north.

The Bungaloos, failing to capture their prey, turned their attention next to any negro that happened to pass. A parade of the down-town streets was begun, and when the crowd sauntered into South Illinois street it met Bluford Williams, a negro employed by the Sentinel. Williams is familiarly known as "Black Annie." A rush was made for him, but Williams darted into the Sentinel building, greatly frightened. Not stopping until he was upstairs, he procured a revolver and returned to the sidewalk, but none of his pursuers could be seen. The whites, after leaving the Sentinel, again marched uptown, where they encountered George Kinslow, a mulatto, who rooms on South Illinois street. It was fortunate for Kinslow that a street car was passing at the time, going at good speed, or he might have suffered at the hands of the determined crowd. He was chased half a block before he caught the car. His escape was followed by many derisive yells and jeers. The next appearance of the whites was near the postoffice, at 11 o'clock, where they espied a negro walking north on Pennsylvania street. Cries of "Let me hit him!" "Kill the skunk!" etc., soon told the negro that he would have to seek a place of shelter. He finally ran into an office building and evaded the crowd.

RAGE RIOT AT GILLSBURG, LA.
Negro Lynched for Usual Crime--- Other Negroes Rise in Arms and 18 are Killed.
New Orleans, Nov. 15.—A special from Kentwood, La., says:

Eighteen negroes were killed at Gillsburg, a small town, twelve miles northeast of this place, in a race riot today. The trouble arose over the lynching of a negro who criminally assaulted a white woman.

Details of the killing are very meagre. It is understood that the assault occurred last evening when the male members of the family were absent. After accomplishing his purpose the negro fled to the woods.

The alarm was given and in a few moments fifty or more citizens responded to the call to arms, and the man hunt was begun. A description of the negro was given and the posse searched the woods all night. They came upon him shortly before noon today and brought him back to the village, where he was fully identified. The posse was composed of a determined set of citizens and they lost no time in getting a rope. They hurriedly placed the string around the negro's neck and he was hauled up on a branch of a tree back of a barn.

From all accounts received here today, it is evident that the black man was popular with the members of his race. When they heard that he had been lynched, they became angry and showed determination to avenge his death. The word was passed around and soon many of the negroes of the village began congregating. They were in an ugly mood, and many of them were armed.

They were out looking for trouble and from all sections they got plenty of it. They started the riot with the whites, and it is reported here tonight that eighteen members of their race were killed. Others were wounded in the riot.

The sheriff, assisted by his lieutenants, made a great effort to suppress the riot and finally succeeded.

Holdenville, I. T., Jan. 28.—A few days ago negro help was employed at some of the hotels in Holdenville and immediately a strong sentiment was manifested and expressed at once against the action of the hotel keepers, and later the negroes were ordered to leave town, which they failed to do. On Saturday night about 11 o'clock some miscreant, in order to frighten them away, threw a dynamite bomb against the small building in the rear of one of the hotels used for servants' quarters, which smashed in the windows, and gave the house a general shaking up and causing a stampede of the negroes, who no longer hesitated about leaving but took the first train out of town.

The explosion of the dynamite caused great excitement, which was augmented by the fact that on the same evening the Frisco express, mail and passenger train had passed through under the guard of a heavily armed posse, and it was reported that the railway people were fearing a hold-up. On hearing the explosion many of the citizens grabbed their revolvers and Winchesters and rushed out expecting to find the bank being looted by a gang of outlaws, but when they reached that financial institution they found their fears without foundation, for the building had not been attacked and of course the cash was still resting in the vaults.

It was the most painfully exciting moment ever experienced in Holdenville, but when it was all over every citizen congratulated himself upon the fact that the worst damage to the town, if any existed, was the loss of the negro help and a few broken window glasses.

Special to The Globe.

joe-scott-montevideo-1903-11-24.A9:
GETS THIRTY YEARS
Joseph Scott, Negro Assailant of Miss Olson, Sentenced on Three Indictments.
Proceedings Occupied Less Than an Hour—Prisoner Expected to Be Hanged.
Special to The Journal. Montevideo. Minn..
Montevideo, Minn., Nov. 25.—Joseph Henry Scott was brought to this place from the Glencoe jail by Sheriff Hartley yesterday afternoon to answer to the charge of three indictments returned by the grand jury—robbery in the first degree, assault in the first degree and burglary in the first degree. A large crowd gathered at the station, but there was no demonstration, and Scott was taken directly to the courthouse, where court was in session.

The indictments were read and he pleaded guilty to all three. Before sentence was passed the judge appointed Attorney Gjerset as the prisoner's legal advisor, and the two had a short conference. The prisoner was given an opportunity to plead in his own behalf. He said he did not intend to injure any one and that he did not know why he did it; that he was sorry he was in court and for the trouble he had caused to others. He asked the court for mercy if there was any to be shown.

He was then given ten years for each of the three indictments, the first at hard labor, a total sentence of thirty years. In less than one hour from the time he arrived in town he was sentenced and in the county jail under a heavy guard.

He was visited in his cell by hundreds of people, and to all he talked freely. To the Journal correspondent he said he was born in Kansas City, Mo., July 20, 1878. He had been married, his wife dying six years ago. His parents were both drowned in the floods last spring. He has a brother living in Oregon and a married sister in Kansas City. He had been a barber at home and also worked at brush-making.

Scott is well read and bright in many ways, while in others he seems deficient. He said he expected to hang when brought here, and is surprised that he was treated so well. The people in general seem well satisfied with the sentence, and even the relatives of the injured girl, Miss Olson, are satisfied that the ends of justice have been met.

Scott was taken to Stillwater at noon to-day. This was the closing chapter of one of the most cruel and brutal crimes in the history of the state.

Miss Olson, while improving, is confined to her bed, being able to sit up only at short intervals.

Happy in the knowledge that he was at last safe from a threatening mob, Joe Scott, the negro who attempted to kill Helen Olson at Watson, Minn., last July, sat in a cell at the county jail last night and related in detail the story of his crime, the first complete confession the negro has made since his capture on the day following the attempted murder.

Scott told how he had landed at the little village of Watson in a box car, which had been sidetracked there, of how he later heard people talking about money while passing the home of Helen Olson, and how he waited until the lights in the house had been extinguished, when he removed a screen and entered the house for the purpose of robbery.

Scott was to have had his trial at Montevideo this week, but when arraigned in court Tuesday afternoon he weakened and pleaded guilty to the charges against him, being immediately sentenced to thirty years in the penitentiary.

Fearing that the mob, which filled the court house and crowded the streets of the town, might attempt to lynch the negro, Sheriff Hartley, assisted by several deputies, brought the negro to St. Paul on the first train which left Montevideo following the disposal of Scott's case.

Even with this precaution a threatening mob followed the party to the train, and Scott felt much easier when he was well out of the mob's sight. Today he will be taken to Stillwater to serve his sentence of thirty years.

Makes Public Confession.

While in the county jail last night Scott sent for a Globe reporter, stating that he desired before going to prison to give a correct account of the crime and the incidents which led up to it. He made no attempt whatever to shield himself, except to reiterate that the crime was not premeditated, but the result of a temporary aberration of the mind.

Scott's statement to The Globe was as follows:

"I've got my sentence now and I want to tell the truth of this case. To begin with, I had just been released from the North Dakota penitentiary, and was beating my way through the country in a box car. I went to sleep and when I awoke I found that the car I was in had been side tracked. I got out and walked over to the stock yards to get a drink of water, and in walking around I passed the Olson house. A number of people were standing in the yard and I heard them say something about money. I needed money, so I decided I would rob the house that night. I kept out of sight until quite late, when I got into the house through a window.

Went Three Times to the House.

"I searched everywhere for money, but I could not find any, so I went up stairs, and finally went into a bed room where two girls were sleeping. One was the Olson girl and the other was a girl named, as I have later learned, Julia Torgenson. When they awoke I demanded money, but they said there was not any in the house. I parleyed with them and finally left. I went back the second time, and after another unsuccessful attempt, I left again. Then for the third time I went back. This time the Olson girl said there was a little money down stairs and she went down with me to get it. The other girl did not come down, and I guess they were both scared, for the last time I went in I took an ax which I had found in the yard. After the girl had given me the money, about $2, I struck her in the head with an ax, after which I called to the girl up stairs to come down, as I had hurt the Olson girl. I then got out of the house and tried to make my escape. I walked all night and the next day I slept in the woods.

"Along in the evening I woke up and saw people riding along the road with guns and rifles. I knew they were looking for me, and when I attempted to get away they saw me, and I started to run. After running down the road I jumped a fence and started across a wheat field, but before I had gone very far I was shot in the arm and had to surrender.

"They kept me in jail at Glencoe for fear that I would me mobbed if taken to Montevideo, for the girl was expected to die. I only went to Montevideo Tuesday, when they were ready for me in court, and when I got sight of the mob I decided that it was best for me to plead guilty."

Scott had no complaint to make of the sentence which had been imposed upon him, but stated that he was sorry he had committed the crime, as he had not intended to injure any one.

The attempted murder of Helen Olson, the twenty-two-year-old daughter of Thomas Olson, occurred on the night of July 17, and attracted much attention at the time, hundreds of people turning out to search for Scott. It was only through the vigilance of the sheriff that the mob was kept from lynching the negro at the time he was captured.

Good advice for Northern people does not often come from South Carolina. But here is some from the Charleston News and Courier. Commenting on a recent case of lynch law at Belleville, Ill., the News and Courier says:

"We have no reproaches for the people of Illinois, however. They will find that the lynching habit will grow upon them, as it has grown upon the people of the commonwealths which have permitted the mob to take the place of the law. WHITECAPS WHIPPED NEGROES NEAR BARWICK.
Quitman, Ga., March 9.—Word reached her to-day of the deeds of a band of whitecaps near Barwick last Friday. They entered the house of Charles Hammons, claiming to have a warrant for him and his son, and took them out in the woods and gave them a severe beating. They then gave the men forty-eight hours to get out of the state.

They attempted to take Lee Wright, but he gave them leg ball, outran them and lay hid in the swamp all night. They finished up by firing into the house of Scott Wilson, fatally wounding his boy. All the victims are said to be respectable negroes, and no reason is known for the whitecaps' action. They were disguised, and none of the party were recognized.

Trouble in Burke County Over Disappearance of Holmes.

Louisville, Ga., May 29.—A telephone message was received here this morning from Stellaville, in Burke county, by Sheriff Farmer, stating that trouble in that district was imminent, and his services were needed. He immediately left for the scene with a deputy.

The trouble arose over the disappearance of a young man, Mr. Dupree Holmes, who is supposed to have been murdered by an old negro, Leroy Gibbons. Mr. Holmes disappeared mysteriously on Tuesday, and has not been seen since.

Gibbons was captured and taken to Stellaville and placed under a guard, which was later overpowered by the friends of the missing young man. Gibbons was taken to the swamp and a rope was put about his neck to bring out the truth of the matter.

His wife was also taken to the woods with him. He protested his innocence, but his wife, after a severe beating, said that he was the murderer. In the meantime Gibbons escaped from the mob and came in and gave himself up and was placed in jail for safe keeping.

The negroes in that vicinity thought that Gibbons had been lynched and became very indignant. After the sheriff arrived upon the scene the excitement abated.

Augusta, May 30.—Telegrams received tonight from Whens and Spread, Ga., show that the escape of the negro, Leroy Gibbons, who was under arrest for the killing of Dupree Holmes, was a genuine escape and that the rumor that he was lynchd was not true.

Story from Louisville.
Louisville, Ga., May 31.—Dupree Holmes, the young man that was supposed to have been murdered on last Tuesday, and for whose body Briar creek has been dragged for miles, came home this morning as well and hearty as he ever was, although his disappearance came near causing the lynching of Leroy Gibbons, a peaceable old negro, and also came near causing race troubles in the Stellaville district.

Holmes says he has heard nothing of it until to-day, and he says he was only a few miles away all the while. His story is that he went to a sawmill in an isolated portion of the district, was taken ill and could not get back until to-day. The old negro, who was in the hands of the mob, dashed from under their guns into the swamp and made his way to Louisville and surrendered to the sheriff, but had to be sent to Macon for safety.

The old negro's wife, who was beaten almost insensible by the mob to secure a confession of the crime, is in a very precarious condition. She says had she not told that her husband had killed Mr. Holmes she believes she would have been killed.

The sheriff has wired that Gibbons be released at Macon and furnished with transportation home.
