HOLMES TURNS UP AT HOME.
HIS STORY EXPLAINING HIS DISAPPEARANCE.
Several Days Ago Holmes Was Missed—Mob Visited Leroy Gibbons, Who Professed His Innocence of Murder—Under the Lash Gibbons' Wife "Confessed" That Her Husband Had Killed Holmes. Gibbons Managed to Make His Escape—Story Told by Holmes.

Augusta, Ga., May 31.—For the past few days there has been a great sensation along the Augusta Southern Railroad in the territory about Stellaville, Wrens, Keysville and extending to Augusta on the one side and to Louisville on the other, over the alleged murder of young Dupree Holmes, member of a well known family, and himself well acquainted in all this territory.

As has been published in the Morning News, he left home last Tuesday morning to collect some money due him from a negro, Leroy Gibbons. Late in the afternoon his horse came home with the saddle, but without the bridle, and two days' searching by friends secured no trace of the missing young man.

Beat the Poor Woman.

Thursday bodies of men determined to find out the truth and went to the home of Leroy Gibbons and demanded to know what had become of Mr. Holmes after he saw him Tuesday. Gibbons declared he had never seen him. The lash was tried as a persuader, and under this Gibbons' wife told a story about Leroy killing Holmes with a hoe, throwing his body over the fence and hauling it away at night in a wagon to throw it in Briar creek.

Saturday night rumors were rife that Leroy Gibbons had been lynched the night before, but it developed that he had got away from the men who had him in charge and made his escape to Louisville, where he gave himself up to the sheriff, protesting his innocence.

In the meantime searching parties have dragegd Briar creek and continued the search for Holmes body, but no trace was found until early this morning, when he walked into his home with no signs of injury on his person.

What Holmes Says.

His story is that after his horse got away from him and ran home, he met up with a man who told him a sawmill some ten miles away was temporarily idle, and he could get some hands there that he needed in his cotton field. He walked to the sawmill, was taken seriously sick and had been there in the camp with the men for the past four or five days, entirely ignorant of the sensation created by his disappearance.

The strange features of the story are that he did not get his horse and ride to the sawmill, instead of walking there, it being ten miles away, and his home not half as far from the place where his horse is said to have left him; also that nobody in the camp should have taken word to his home about Holmes being seriously sick there.

But the facts are that Dupree Holmes is safe at home, while a poor negro woman has been cruelly beaten to force a confession from her, and an innocent man was not lynched simply because he had the good fortune to break away into the swamp and elude his guard.
leroy-gibbons-matthews-1903-05-28.A9:
THE CASE OF LEROY GIBBONS.
A great deal of interest has been manifested in the case of Leroy Gibbons of Jefferson county in this state. Gibbons came very near being the victim of a mob's vengeance, and his case emphasizes in the strongest manner the danger there is in lynch law to innocent persons suspected of crime.

According to the story told in our dispatches Dupree Holmes started for the home of Leroy Gibbons last Tuesday for the purpose of collecting money which Gibbons owed him. He was on horseback. That was the last seen of him until last Sunday. His horse returned to the Holmes residence the same day without a bridle, and there were at once suspicions of foul play, in view of the absence of evidence of an accident. A party of citizens visited the home of Gibbons who stoutly denied that Mr. Holmes had been at his place. He was arrested, however, and attempts made to compel him to confess. That failing the lash was applied to his wife. Under the pain of the punishment inflicted upon her she said that her husband had killed Mr. Holmes with a hoe, and that he had carried the body away and concealed it. That evidence seemed so positive that it is probable that few doubted that Gibbons had killed Mr. Holmes.

On Sunday Mr. Holmes returned to his home. It seems that his horse got away from him, and that he went on to a saw-mill some ten miles distant where he expected to be able to hire some hands that he needed. He was taken ill there and, instead of sending word home as to his whereabouts, had remained at the saw-mill camp until he recovered. He had not heard anything about the excitement that his disappearance had caused.

Of course every man that was in the party that was hunting for Mr. Holmes would have profoundly regretted it if the old negro man, Gibbons, had been lynched, and doubtless they regret the punishment that was inflicted upon the wife of Gibbons. But the fact remains that the old colored woman was so harshly treated that she told a falsehood that came very near costing him his life. Gibbons himself was saved from the mob by being sent by the sheriff to the jail at Macon.

The conclusion to be drawn from this case is that the law should be permitted to take its course on all occasions. The courts will deal with those who are accused of heinous offenses much more satisfactorily than a mob can, and are much less likely to make mistakes. A mob may think it has convincing evidence against the person charged with crime, but the evidence may be worthless. The wife's statement in the case of Gibbons seemed conclusive, and yet it was totally false. It was made under fear of death. She had only one thought, and that was to say something that would appease the mob and thus save her own life. Mob law is full of danger to innocent persons suspected of crime, and all right thinking people should frown upon it. In that way a public sentiment will be formed that will put a check upon it.
leroy-gibbons-matthews-1903-05-28.A13:
The Danger of Lynching.
Leroy Gibbons may thank his lucky star that he is alive today. His experience shows the outrage and danger of mob rule, and the little chance an innocent man has with circumstantial evidence against him at a lynchers' court. The case in question is reported from Jefferson county, Ga., and it has attracted unusual attention.

Gibbons is a Negro. He was under financial obligations to Dupree Holmes and a week ago Holmes started to the former's house to make a collection. He was on horse back. He did not return that night and when the animal galloped back after dark without saddle or bridle, foul play was suspected. The Negro was arrested. He professed innocence of any wrong doing. Not being able to learn anything from him, friends of the white man applied the lash to the wife of Gibbons in the brutal hope that she would make a confession. And she got busy with her tongue just as soon as the pain became unbearable. To save herself from punishment the wife swore that the husband had killed Holmes with a hoe. This appeared to be evidence enough for the mob. The Negro, however, was not lynched, but he came near taking the short end of the rope.

Imported Colored Waiters from Terre Haute Forced to Leave the Mining Town in a Hurry.
NO VIOLENCE WAS OFFERED
NEGROES PLACED IN A WAGON AMID CHEERS OF TWO THOUSAND,
Then Driven in the Direction of Vigo County-Quiet Restored in Short Time.
LINTON, Ind., July 6.—The race hatred epidemic seems to be spreading. This city had a violent attack of the prevailing disease to-night, and if the sentiment displayed by a crowd of 2,000 people is evidence of the real feeling of the city negroes hereafter will shun Linton. There was no serious rioting or violence, the crowd merely driving a number of imported colored waiters out of the city simply because they were colored.

A lodge of Elks was organized here this evening and the town was filled with visiting members of the order from Terre Haute, Vincennes, Bedford, Bloomington and other neighboring cities. The hosts of the visitors desired to make things as pleasant as possible for their brothers, and also hoped to show them that they knew how to spread a feast. With this end in view a special caterer was engaged at Terre Haute to prepare the banquet that was to be one of the features of the programme this evening.

The Terre Haute caterer brought several colored waiters with him. This is one of the cities in which no negro is allowed, and when the caterer and his assistants arrived on the scene it was only a short time until there were street-corner consultations over what was to be done with the colored men who had innocently been brought to the city. Discussion of the question was not confined to a few radical negro haters, but it became general, and by nightfall the streets were filled with 2,000 people and excitement was at a high pitch. Self-delegated leaders addressed the throng that rapidly increased in size and a vote was taken as to what should be done about asking the colored men to leave. The slogan of the crowd was "Peace if possible, but force if necessary."

A committee was appointed to wait on the caterer and have the colored men leave at once. The waiters needed no urging to leave, for the crowd seemed to mean business. A covered wagon was secured with little delay and the luckless negroes were driven post haste in the direction of the city on the banks of the Wabash, while the crowd cheered. The people soon dispersed and the town assumed its customary quiet.

Although the affair somewhat marred the pleasure of the gathering of the Elks, the work proceeded as if nothing had happened. While the streets were filled with hundreds of people, it is said that there were many in the crowd who did not approve of the deportation, but would not do anything to stop it.

An Associated Press dispatch says: "The appearance of eight Terre Haute negroes in Linton to-day caused a demonstration, in which the men narrowly escaped death. Alex. Sanderson, a Terre Haute caterer, was employed to serve the banquet at the institution of a new lodge of the Elks. He took his cook and waiters with him, and while the lodge work in the hall was going on several hundred miners assembled in the street and threatened to dynamite the hall unless the negroes were sent out of town. The eight colored men were hurried into a cab and driven to Jasonville, where they were put on the train for Terre Haute. Six policemen hung on the carriage and beat back the crowd while the negroes were driving out of town."

TUESDAY EVENING, JULY 7, 1903.
THE NEWSPAPERS still teem with dispatches from various sections representing lynchings, race riots, &c. Barely had the trouble passed away which recently convulsed Wilmington, Del. when similar disturbances broke out in other places, and Evansville, Ind., became a storm centre. The cloud still hangs over that place while another has settled over Linton, Ind., where the appearance of eight Terre Haute negroes yesterday afternoon was the cause of a demonstration in which the men narrowly escaped with their lives. They were engaged by a caterer who was preparing a banquet in a hall for a lodge of Elks, when several hundred miners assembled in the street and threatened to dynamite the hall unless the negroes were sent out of town. Intense feeling against negroes has been fostered in Linton for seven years, and in that time not a negro has been allowed to live in that town. Asbury Park, N. J., supposed to be a conservative and quiet place, was in a ferment yesterday when an attempt was made to lynch three negroes who were charged with driving a vehicle over a white woman who was riding a bicycle. Many people are being cast into serious reveries at the rapid growth of mob law in the United States. It is no longer a sectional distemper, nor are the cases sporadic, and the outcome is naturally viewed with apprehension.
linton-linton-1903-07-06.A3:
NEGROES CAUSE ANOTHER RIOT
ARE DRIVEN OUT OF LINTON, IND., AND POLICEMEN HANG TO CAB WHILE BEATING BACK THE PURSUING MOB OF WHITES.
Linton, Ind., July 6.—The appearance of eight Terre Haute negroes in Linton today caused a demonstration in which the men narrowly escaped death. Alex Sanderson, a Terre Haute caterer, was employed to serve the banquet at the institution of a new lodge of the Elks. He took his cooks and waiters with him and while the lodge work in the hall was going on several miners assembled in the street and threatened to dynamite the hall unless the negroes were sent out of town.

The eight colored men were hurried into a cab and driven to Jasonville where they were put on the train for Terre Haute. Six policemen hung on the carriage and beat back the crowd while the negroes were driven out of town.

The intense feeling here against the negroes has been fostered for several years and in that time not a negro has been allowed to live in Linton.

In 1896 a coal company imported 300 negroes to take the places of strikers in one of the mines here. The negroes organized a company and drilled with rifles on the streets. John W. Sanborn.
A great warm heart has ceased to beat. A powerful mind has passed from earthly activities. A strong, sound body, in which dwelt a noble soul, goes to its long resting place. John W. Sanborn is dead. He was a great man and he was a good man. He commanded the respect of all who knew him. He was personally beloved by more people than any other citizen of New Hampshire. In physique, in bodily strength, in natural mental endowments and in the powers that are developed by constant application and ever faithful and well directed endeavor, he was a perfect type of the greatness and nobility which were the characteristics of the men and women who settled and developed New Hampshire and gave it its proud position in the sisterhood of states.

He had little school education. He had no money except what he earned. He had no influential relatives. He had no opportunities that were not open to every other New Hampshire boy seventy years ago. He began at a very early age to earn his living. He commenced his business career by purchasing with what he had saved from his wages a beef creature and peddling the carcass in a wagon which he borrowed. From this he went on buying and selling cattle and sheep until he was the best known and most successful drover in the eastern part of the state. In the mean time he had acquired and improved a large farm, which was his homestead until he died, and his excellent judgment, his perfect honesty, his kindness and his tact made him the most trusted and influential man in Carroll county, where he had a personal acquaintance with nearly every one.

In 1871 the Portsmouth, Great Falls & Conway railroad had been pushed by slow stages to North Conway and was then leased to the Eastern New Hampshire corporation for 69 years. The disasters that befell the Eastern during the next four years wrecked the Great Falls & Conway, and as that branch was not taking money enough to pay running expenses, and its rolling stock was attached by creditors, it was practically abandoned. Mr. Sanborn, who was then about fifty-two years of age, had had no experience in railroading and knew nothing of the details of the business, but he had been influential in getting the road built and was intensely interested in having it operated, because it was the only line through his county and all his people were dependent upon it. He therefore went to Boston and obtained from the managers of the Eastern, who confessed their inability to run it, permission to take charge of it and do what he could to put a train service upon it. He returned home, receipted to the sheriff for a decrepit locomotive and a few old cars, hired the trainmen, agreeing to pay them himself, bought wood for fuel, giving his own notes for it, went over the o'd track and picked up the scrap iron and took it to Somersworth, where he swapped it for a few tools with which to repair the worn-out track, and soon had trains running over it.

He was then superintendent of the Division, which has been his title nearly ever since, though most of his work has been in broader fields. At that time the stock of the corporation was quoted at a dollar a share. He proceeded to create business by making it for the advantage of manu-

facturers and landlords to locate upon the line by running excursions to Boston and by coaxing summer travelers over it, and steadily built it up and made it a profitable property, until it was leased, with the Eastern, to the Boston & Maine and its stock was in demand at $118 a share. Subsequently, when Frank Jones was president of the Boston & Maine, Mr. Sanborn was the general superintendent and executive officer, and ever since has had general charge of the interests of that corporation in New Hampshire. In all the litigation and legislation of the past twenty years he has been recognized as the Boston & Maine representative, organizer and manager, and its success in working out its far-reaching policies, protecting itself against assaults and strengthening its position is rightfully and cheerfully credited to him by the officers and stockholders of the corporation and the public.

It was a position of tremendous responsibilty and power, but he was qualified for it as was no other man. He was not a lawyer but he had a legal mind and his experience gave him a grasp of and insight into railroad legislation which made him a master in that line. Said the late John H. George, the ablest lawyer of his time, to the writer: "I would rather have the judgment of John W. Sanborn upon a bill affecting railroad interests than that of any lawyer in the state," and this was the general opinion.

He was a born organizer. He seldom made a mistake in selecting his assistants. He was always wise in placing them. He was the most skillful and successful of harmonizers. His forces were never distracted by feuds or weakened by jealousies. However little they liked each other his men worked together as if they were of one mind, and if his opponents were needed he often brought them to his support. He knew how to manage men and do things.

He was always prudent. He never did too much. He was never afraid. He was tireless and indefatigable. He was honest and frank. He deceived no one. He was above trickery of any kind. He had common sense of the highest order. Above all he was true. He was a New Hampshire man and was always loyal to the state. Nothing could tempt him to a course which he did not sincerely believe was for the benefit of New Hampshire and its people. He never forgot his friends or failed to seek opportunities to serve them. He never needed to be reminded of any obligations he was under to any one. He placed nearly every one with whom he was associated under obligations to him. In the service of the great corporation: he entirely divorced himself from his own personal interests. He had neither ambition nor greed to satisfy. He never used the great power he wielded to nominate or elect any one, to promote any enterprise, to defeat any scheme, to accomplish any result that he did not think was for the advantage of the state and the Boston & Maine railroad, for which he stood first, last and all the time.

He was approachable and companionable. His judgments were just. His private life was pure. His word was never broken. These qualities not only made him strong but they endeared him to all who knew him. Once, after the consolidation of the Boston & Maine and Concord & Montreal, the question arose, who should have the management of the combined interests in this state, and one man who knew him said, "The legislature and the people of New Hampshire will do more for the love they bear Uncle John Sanborn than they will do for all the money all the lobbies of both roads can distribute;" and this was true. People often did what "Uncle John" asked them not more because they believed in him or felt under obligations to him and those he represented than because they loved him.

He never sought a political office; but he had positive political convictions and was a power in any party with which he acted. During the war of the rebellion he was a member of the house of representatives and of the governor's council, and although a Democrat was a stanch supporter of the Union cause and devoted himself unreservedly to the great task of furnishing New Hampshire's quota and caring for her soldiers. Afterwards he was president of the state senate and was a member of the constitutional convention. In 1896 he could not bring himself to support Bryan, and having reached the conclusion that it was his duty to vote for McKinley went openly to the Republicans, taking with him a large following.

He was a generous man and public spirited. The village of Sanbornville, where he died, was created by him, and the town of Wakefield is greatly indebted to him for its prosperity.

He lived 81 years and died as he hoped to die, worn out in the service of his state, his corporation, his friends and his fam

Prisoner Taken from Moultrie to Prevent Lynching.

Chicago Negroes Are Nearly Lynched for a Murder.
CHICAGO, Nov. 1.—The celebration of Halloween was responsible for the killing of the chief of police of Morgan Park and a threatened race war early today. It was only after a desperate struggle between the police and an armed mob of enraged whites that a lynching was prevented.

A woman's Halloween prank started the trouble, which ended in the killing of George A. Airie; chief of police of Morgan Park, by Mack Wiley, a young negro. Mrs. James Payne, who is a sister of Wiley, and three friends started out for a lark and while they were overturning a lumber pile, it is said, the woman was struck by Chief Airie. The negroes went for reinforcements and upon their return a second meeting with Airie resulted in a fight, in which he was stabbed in the neck by Wiley.

A crowd of half a hundred men and boys marched to the Morgan Park jail, where four of the negroes had been locked up. The prisoners were rescued by the officers and taken to the Englewood jail, but not until they had been severely cut and bruised with sticks and stones.

CHICAGO, Nov. 1.—Chief of Police George Airie of Morgan Park was shot and killed last night by a negro whom he had arrested for playing Halloween pranks. The negro and three companions, also colored, were arrested and placed in the town lockup.

The news of the killing spread through the suburb with rapidity and soon crowds of men and boys gathered in front of the village hall and it was with the greatest difficulty that they were prevented from using violence. Fear that the friends of the dead man would break into the jail and attack the negroes led the police to take the prisoners to the Englewood jail for safekeeping. They will be held pending the coroner's inquest.

The negroes were cut and bruised by stones and clubs in the hands of the mob.

LYNCHING PREVENTED.
Chicago Police Rescue Four Negroes from Mob of Morgan Park Citizens.
Chicago, Ill., Nov. 2.—Timely interference of the Chicago police in the affairs of the village of Morgan Park yesterday was all that saved Cook county from the disgrace that attends a lynching. The police were able to rescue from the beleaguered lock-up at Morgan Park four negroes accused of participation in the murder of George A. Airey, the village chief of poliice. When they arrived on the scene a mob of residents of Morgan Park, Harvey and Blue Island surrounded the village prison and clamored for vengeance against the negroes.

Once, before the Chicago police arrived, the mob had forced its way into the village hall in which the lockup is located. Led by John and Robert Airey, brother and son of the murdered chief, the crowd swept up to the bars of the cell in which were the four negroes and women arrested with them. The mob had nearly reached the prisoners when a patrol wagon loaded with officers drove up in front of the hall. The Chicago policemen accomplished what the local officials had been unable to do. The mob was driven back from the rear door of the hall and in another minute the four frightened negroes were hurried into the patrol wagon and whisked away to Chicago and out of danger.

In the Englewood police station they confessed their share in the murder of Chief Airey and were locked up to await the verdict of the coroner's jury.

The chief lost his life while trying to arrest a gang of disorderly negroes Saturday night.

CHICAGO, Nov. 3.—Rage over the murder of Chief of Police George Airri has caused the citizens of Morgan Park, a suburb of this city, to bill the town with posters ordering the negroes of the town to leave at once. At a secret meeting last evening it was decided by certain persons to clear the town of its colored population.

Despite the efforts of Mayor George Prentiss and his twelve deputies to prevent any action the posters were put up. The negroes to-day were stricken with terror. They began to leave. Several families went away taking what belongings they could.

NELSON PIXTON, WHITE IS STABBED BY A NEGRO
Assault Occurred in James Stevens' Saloon.
LYNCHING WAS THREATENED
Witnesses Infuriated by the Cold- Blooded Attack, But Barten- der Intervened.
Nelson Pixton, a tinner, was probably fatally stabbed by Frederick W. Williams, colored, in a fight in the poolroom in the rear of James Stevens' saloon, at Eighth and E Streets northwest. That the negro was not lynched by the infuriated gathering attracted to the scene of the trouble is undoubtedly due to the prompt action of the proprietor of the saloon, who took the negro out of sight of the mob and placed him in a rear room until the police arrived. Williams was taken to the First Precinct station and Pixton to the Emergency Hospital.

Pixton and five or six friends were in the poolroom most of the afternoon, and were engaged in a game of pool when Williams entered. An altercation was started, in which the white men and the negro were calling each other names. The negro says the white men started it, and the white men blame the colored man. Blows were exchanged, and the negro was knocked down.

A Vicious Attack.

But, whatever the provocation, it is said by witnesses that the attack was particularly vicious and cold-blooded. Williams is said to have thrust the knife in the left side of his victim, turned it in the wound, pulled it out and wiped it off, closed it and shoved it into his pocket, while half a dozen spectators looked on too much unnerved to make a move.

When the friends of Pixton recovered they grabbed the negro and attempted to drag him outside the saloon. Stevens interfered and by a determined attitude gained possession of the colored man and took him into a back room, where Williams immediately began to protest that he had only used the knife in self-defense.

Williams' nose was bleeding profusely and this blood, mingling with that of his white victim, seemed to infuriate the gathering mob and shouts of "Lynch the bloody nigger" were set up and repeated again and again. In the meantime the police arrived and this had the effect of quieting the demonstration.

Three-Inch Wound.

At the Emergency Hospital the physicians say Pixton is seriously wounded. The knife with which he was stabbed inflicted a three-inch wound, just below the heart, and made a two-inch puncture in the stomach. Fearing that the intestines were also punctured, the physicians made a thorough examination, and found that they were not injured. After sewing up the wound in the stomach and the one in the side, the physicians placed Pixton in a ward where he is now detained. His home is near Schultzer Park northwest.

Policemen Levi and Wolfe took Williams into custody. He protested his innocence, but as a knife similar to the one described by the witnesses was found in his pocket he was locked up and a charge entered against him.

Frederick Williams Accused of Stabbing Nelson Pixton.

George Holland was arrested Friday and when confronted with certain points of evidence against him he confessed and implicated six more men. Later Ed Mosely told the officers that he saw the murder committed and was afraid to tell it and he was also taken in charge.

According to Holland's confession the negroes were in Pembroke on Saturday Nov. 14 and saw the stranger display a roll of money and watched him when he went to R. F. Chilton's farm and camped in the woods. He built a fire and went to sleep. The negroes during the night crept upon him and Holland says Meredith dealt the sleeping man a murderous blow with the pick handle afterwards found in the leaves. The body quivered and to complete the work George Holland sprang upon the dying man and cut his throat. All of the gang took part in searching and robbing the body. The spoils were then divided and the murderers then disfigured the dead man's face by cutting away the flesh and burying it in the ground. They lacerated the throat, cut off the ears and mutilated the body. The clothes were slashed and torn, the shoes taken off and burned and the body dragged to the pile of rails some distance away and concealed where it was afterwards found When found it had been rooted about by hogs and had the appearance of having been partially devoured.

The details of the murder were published in the Kentuckian and attracted attention all over the State. Gov. Beckham offered a reward of $250 for the capture and conviction of the murderers. County Judge Fowler offered $50 and these amounts were supplemented by the people of Pembroke, who subscribed $100 to a reward fund.

A glove dropped near the scene by Frank Meredith, alias Merriweather, was the first clew discovered and he was kept under watch. George Holland's actions also excited suspicions and it was finally decided to take him in charge, with the result given above.

The eight men heavily manacled with trace chains, were brought to jail here Sunday and are now in custody.

The identity of the victim is still a mystery. The man was a stranger and there is no very great excitement over the matter and there is not believed to be any danger of mob law, since the conviction of the murderers is necessary to secure the $400 reward for their capture. The murder was a most atrocious one, and if the right men are in custody, and the indications are strongly in favor of the belief that no mistake has been made, there is an excellent chance for a wholesale hanging in Christian county.

The nine negro prisoners charged with the murder of an unknown man at Pembroke Nov. 14, who were in jail here, were taken to Madisonville Thursday at midnight for safe keeping. There were rumors of mob violence, though no danger was visible on the surface of things, and they were taken away to be on the safe side. The negroes were taken to Madisonville by Sheriff Davis and four deputies and were gone before any one knew of the plan to move them.

ALL INDICTED.
Pembroke Negroes Charged With Murder and Conspiracy.
Trial of the Accused Set for Today and Will Probably Consume Two Weeks.
The special grand jury impaneled for the purpose of investigating the murder of the unknown white man near Pembroke, returned an indictment Wednesday morning against all nine of the negroes in jail charged with the crime. The indictment charges them with willful murder committed in manner and form as follows:

That said George Holland, Ed Holland, Frank Meriwether, Frank Massie, Frank Sherman, Ed Moseley, William Garrott, Charles Finch and Dick Carney did in this county and state, aforesaid, on the 20th day of November, 1903, and before the finding of this indictment unlawfully, willfully, maliciously and with malice aforethought, kill, slay and murder a white man, to this grand jury unknown, and in pursuance of said conspiracy the said Frank Meriwether, George Holland and Frank Sherman did then and there unlawfully, wilfully, feloniously and with malice aforethought kill and murder the said unknown white man in the following manner:

That the said Frank Meriwether struck, beat and wounded him, with an ax handle bludgeon or other deadly weapon; that the said George Holland and Frank Sherman cut, stabbed and wounded him with knives or other sharp instruments or weapons, from which said striking, beating, cutting, and wounding he, the said unknown white man, did then and there presently die. That Dick Carney, Frank Massie, William Garrott, Chas. Finch, Ed Moseley and Ed Holland were then and there personally present and did then and there unlawfully, willfully and feloniously and with malice aforethought, aid, assist, abet, counsel, advise and encourage the said Meriwether, George Holland and Sherman to kill and murder the said unknown white man as aforesaid and which said killing was done in pursuance of the conspiracy aforesaid. That the said unknown white man, was killed and murdered as aforesaid.

Shortly after the bill was returned the prisoners were brought into court. The Commonwealth's Attorney asked that time be given in order to summon other witnesses in the case and the trial was set for this morning at 10 o'clock.

R. N. Lander, col., who represents seven of the men, stated that he thought he would be ready at the time fixed for entering the trial. Mr. John Feland, representing two of the prisoners, Charles Finch and Ed Moseley, announced ready, but asked a separate trial for his clients. This was granted and the two men will not be tried with the other seven. If Attorney Lander's clients ask for separate trials the case will necessarily be long drawn out. More than twenty witnesses were examined by the grand jury and there will probably be about fifty in all.

The thirty men summoned as petit jurors were on hand when court opened and were dismissed until this morning, with the instruction to consider themselves impaneled.

Judges C. H. Bush and Jas. Breathitt will assist in the prosecution.

Death Sentence for First Pair of Pembroke Negroes.
Jury Out Three Hours, After Nine Hours of Argument---Verdict Meets With General Approval.
CHAS. FINCH NOW ON TRIAL FOR HIS LIFE.
At 10:30 o'clock Wednesday the jury took the case in the trial of George Holland and Richard Carney, two of the Pembroke murderers, and at 1:30 p. m. the jury returned a verdict of death for both defendants. Dr. Jno. P. Bell was foreman of the jury and the decision was arrived at without any trouble whatever. The jury organized without delay and read over the instructions carefully twice. A vote was then taken by dividing in the room and all stepped to the "guilty" side of the room. Then the jurors decided to go to dinner and finish their work afterwards. When they met again, one ballot was sufficient to decide the fate of the two men and the verdict was soon brought in. The prisoners received it without change of countenance.

The jurors were as follows: Dr. Jno, P. Bell, Thos. J. Baynham, Richard Ray, J. F. Boyd, Harvey Hight, Andy Estes, Amos Robinson, W. G. Word, Travis McCord, Monroe Bullard, J. J. Bowen, Jno. C. White.

The verdict was received by the large crowd in the court room without any demonstration.

The verdict was confidently expected and anything short of the death sentence would have met with strong popular disapproval. The men convicted are two of the ring-leaders. Carney is the man who fixed up the scheme of murder, when he saw the stranger expose his roll of money in the saloon. He is a Tennessee negro, who has lived in Pembroke about two years. He is a long, ungainly brown negro, with a short beard over parts of his face. He has the appearance of being a hardened criminal.

George Holland is low and very black. He was raised by the Holland family, or is a descendant of Holland slaves who were freed 40 years ago. He confessed that he cut the victim's throat after he had been clubbed by Frank Merriwether, but on the stand he repudiated his sworn confession.

The Speeches.

The argument in the case began Tuesday morning. County Attorney O. H. Anderson made the first speech and was followed by Judge C. H. Bush, also for the prosecution. Both speeches were able arguments, covering all the points in the bloody tragedy. In the afternoon Frank H. Ford, col., spoke for the defense. His effort was a creditable one, delivered in a style that showed him to be a speaker of no mean ability.

—JANUARY 15, 1904—
WHEN THE LAW FAILS.
It is announced that the special term of circuit court called for the purpose of trying the nine negroes charged with murder, may adjourn leaving two-thirds of them untried. According to the evidence before the grand jury and according to the confessions of several of them, all are equally guilty and public sentiment demands that all be speedily brought to trial. The people of Pembroke and other portions of the county have with commendable forbearance restrained the mob sentiment everywhere apparent, hoping that for once the law would be equal to the emergency and that the punishment inflicted upon the guilty wretches would be swift and snare. The first trial consumed nearly ten days of the court's valuable time, with delay everywhere interfering with the ends of justice. The law permits separate trials and the court was of course powerless to hasten matters. Lawyers who might have spoken at night, preferred to speak the next day, and the jury that might have been on hand Wednesday had to be sent for Thursday, at the loss of a day. These tardy movements of the law are exasperating to the people, not in this instance alone, but in nearly every case, and it is no wonder that the law is so often brushed aside and that the sovereign will of an outraged public supplants with mob law the farcical attempts to punish crime in the regular way. Court officers perhaps do the best they can with legal obstacles everywhere interfering with the dispatch of business. The failure of a witness to be on hand, the neglect of a sheriff to have jurors present, the indisposition or business engagements of an attorney, are all regarded as proper grounds for delay in the most important cases. With a human life at stake, there can be no indecent haste, and with nine cases to try and a week given to each trial, it is not possible to try all in less than two months. With six cases to be carried to the regular terms, and one of them tried each term, it may be two years before we hear the last of as bloody a murder as ever disgraced civilization. The Goebel assassination, the Coffey murder and other cases, too numerous to mention, show how murder cases may be kept in the courts for years, until witnesses die off and the crimes are forgotten. What is true of the law in Kentucky, is true everywhere, and while this is allowed to remain thus, there will be a growing contempt for the laws
flowed to remain thus, there will be a growing contempt for the laws that are powerless to punish crime. If the people arise in their might and take the law into their own hands in all parts of the country, too often it may be, the law itself is to blame.

If in this case the convicted and indicted assassins lying in jail at public expense are taken out and lynched, it will be because the law was tried and found wanting in the prompt punishment of crime and the protection of life and property.

It is stated that the remnants of the historic battleflag of the Fourteenth Mississippi regiment will be brought to the annual reunion of the Confederate veterans in Jackson during the early part of June. This flag, only a small portion of which is left, has quite an interesting history. Its original decoration was a likeness of Jefferson Davis and the Goddess of Liberty on one side, while on the other was a serpent coiled around an eagle's nest. The flag was carried by Mr. Andrew Payne until he was captured at Fort Donelson, and even then he did not part with it, but managed to conceal the tattered remnants of the banner in his coat lining and kept it there without discovery until he was exchanged six months later. He still has the remnants in his possession and expects to attend the Jackson reunion and exhibit the precious relic to his old comrades.

MOBHLE, Ala., April 12.—The town of Holy Springs, Miss., was excited last night by an attempt of a mob to lynch the two negro murderers held there under sentence. Solomon Glasgow, a negro preacher, murdered a young white boy near that place whom he had been waiting upon and attempted to burn the body.

The negro was convicted of the crime and sentenced to be hanged on last Friday. The execution of sentence was stayed because of an appeal. Charles Strickland had murdered another negro and was under sentence of death.

When a mob appeared last night Sheriff McWilliams disguised his prisoners and escaped through the crowd, the condemned men mingling with the others.

The mob found the son of the Sheriff and forced him to give up the keys and when they found that the prisoners had been spirited away rushed upon the boy, demanding to know where they were. They then demanded permission to search the home of the Sheriff, which they did. The escape of the prisoners was made to the State penitentiary at Jackson.

Jackson, May 20.—The supreme court of Mississippi has adjourned until next October. Only a few unimportant cases were left pending on the docket when the adjournment took place, and the session has been a very notable one in the number and importance of cases, both civil and criminal, disposed of.

Two death sentences were pronounced at the final sitting, both to take place at Holly Springs in Marshall county on the 30th day of June. The first was that of Solomon Glascoe, a negro who assassinated a young white man named Neill Jones, a short time since. The weapon used was an axe, and the negro slipped up behind Jones in the darkness. An attempt was made to lynch him after the arrest, and his neck saved only by the shrewdness of Sheriff McWilliams who successfully eluded his pursuers, passing among them with the prisoner and getting out of the county. The death sentence and its final affirmation is a good illustration of the quickness of Mississippi justice, as the crime was committed only a few weeks ago.

The second death sentence was that of Charles Strickland, who murdered a deputy sheriff named Cal. Thompson. The crime occurred in 1896, and Thompson had been to the negro's house to place him under arrest, when the latter fired through the doorway and shot the officer dead. He escaped to Arkansas and was captured only a few months ago.

A celebrated case decided by the court was that of H. H. Rogers vs. state from the circuit court of Neshoba county. Rogers was tried and convicted of murder of Tom A. Byrd, a brother of Conrgessman Adam Byrd, member of congress from the fifth district, and the case has attracted much attention on account of the prominence of the families involved. The casus belli was a young woman whose chastity had been brought into question, and the shooting was one of those events which take place with startling quickness when a woman's honor is at stake and men's passions are inflamed. After a long and hard-fought trial Rogers was convicted and given a life term in the penitentiary.

NEW ORLEANS, June 30.--Sol Glasgow and Charles Strickland were hanged legally to-day at Holly Springs, Miss. Both were negroes and were put to death for the murder of whites. TWO BLACKS PAY PENALTY.
Solomon Glascow and Chas. Strickland Hanged at Holly Springs Yesterday.
Holly Springs, Miss., June, 30.—Chas. Strickland and Solomon Glasco, negroes, were hanged this morning, the former at fifteen minutes past 11 oclock, the latter at seven minutes to 12. Both died a few moments after the trap was sprung.

Strickland denied to the end that he fired the shot which killed his victim, and in a short speech warned all the colored people to attend strictly to their own matters, and said that a note was the cause of his death. He became hysterical and boasted of not being afraid to die, laughing and facetiously referring to the noose as a necktie. The black cap and rope were placed over his head and neck, the trap dropped and his soul took its flight.

Glasco was hanged a short while later, but had not seen the execution of Strickland, awaiting in a closed carriage his return at the engine of death.

Not a Murder, Perhaps.
before going to press next week
Just before going to press last week news came to Woodbury that a murder had been committed in Swedesboro, the murderer being Thomas Vaughn, (not Baughu) as printed last week, who had shot his wife Martha, on the street. The supposed murderer was brought to Woodbury, and the wounded woman taken to Cooper Hospital. Later a 'phone message came to Woodbury that the woman had died before reaching the hospital. The only accuracy in the report was as to the fate of the woman, she did not die, as the 'phone told, but late reports indicate that she is on the road to recovery, with a 32-calibre bullet in her brain.

Soon after being received at the hospital the X-Ray was employed to locate the bullet and it was found to be in the lower back of the head, embedded in the brain. The doctors gave no hope for her recovery, and her death was anticipated. But she lives, and from recent reports is recovering all her faculties. Should she live one year and a day, her husband cannot be tried for murder in the first degree, but for homicide or aggravated assault.

Officers have been looking up the woman's past and find that she is the daughter of James and Annie Burge, very respectable colored people of 2739 Gordon street, Philadelphia. She is 19 years of age, and when she proposed to leave home to seek employment in Swedesboro, her father, who by trade is a hod carrier, told her she would have to take her choice between his home and her proposed course. But she went, and this is her reward. The officers say that her parents' home is the best appointed habitation of colored people they ever saw, and her parents are above the average of colored people in refinement.
